newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian clocks go back...then forward again.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian clocks go back...then forward again.

text.p: Bosnia's Moslems, Serbs and Croats couldn't even agree what time it was on Sunday.
By government decree, clocks went back an hour on Sunday in Moslem-controlled parts of Bosnia, while the rest of the country -- and of Europe -- stuck with the old time.

But later in the day the Sarajevo government, realising that it had unilaterally ended summer time a month early, backtracked and told its citizens to put their clocks forward again by an hour on Monday.
When Sarajevans sat down for Sunday lunch at noon, watches in the Serb republic town of Pale a few kilometres away read one o'clock.
In the ethnically divided city of Mostar, Croats on the west bank of the Neretva were an hour ahead of Moslems on the east bank.
This despite the fact that Moslems and Croats are partners in a federation governing 51 per cent of Bosnia.

"If this is a preview of what we can expect from a unified Bosnia I think the country might be better off going back to war," joked one Sarajevan who was at a loss to explain how or why his government had decided to go it alone on a time change.
Officials contacted in Croat and Serb-controlled parts of Bosnia said they would wait until late October and set their clocks back along with the rest of western Europe.
"Would you rather be in step with Europe or in step with the Moslems in Sarajevo?" said one Croat official in Mostar who asked not to be named.
Because it was Sunday, no one was available at the Ministry of Social Policy, which made the decision, to explain.

But by late in the afternoon -- don't ask what time -- Bosnian state radio announced without much fanfare that clocks which had been set back an hour on Sunday should be moved forward one hour on Monday.
The broadcast said a number of European countries had fallen into the same trap and that all would now be turning the clocks back an hour in unison on October 27th.
